segments.title: Trade and strategic depth drive Korea's destroyer fleet
segments.body: South Korea's blue-water expansion extends a navy that still has to operate in the peninsula's littoral waters. The fortified land border makes the sea a route around fixed defences, as the Incheon landings demonstrated during the Korean War. Wider naval reach helps block an opponent from exploiting that route while giving South Korea more defensive depth and power-projection options. It also protects the maritime trade on which major Korean exporters and the national economy depend. Destroyers, frigates, amphibious ships, and possible carrier aviation all answer those connected geographic and economic demands.

evidence.note: The opening presents South Korea as a blue-water navy case and introduces the destroyer program after the Ulsan frigates.
Korea's peninsular geography and the Incheon landing show why the sea provides strategic depth, while global trade and major Korean corporations add economic demands for naval protection.

segments.summary: Blue-water destroyers extend South Korea's defensive depth beyond its fortified land border and protect the maritime trade that supports its economy.

segments.title: Domestic design teams adapt foreign systems to Korean needs
segments.body: The Ulsan-class frigates were South Korea's largest domestically built warships before KDX. Concern after the Vietnam War about national self-support and protection pushed the country toward domestic naval capability. Major industrial capacity was already available, but design independence required teams with military and naval expertise. They had to judge which American and other foreign ideas fit Korean waters, the exclusive economic zone, force structure, and strategic needs. The aim was to integrate and modify imported systems around national requirements. The US Constellation frigate program provides a comparison: an intended difference of about 15% from the FREMM parent design became an estimated 15% commonality, or 30% on a generous estimate. Even a capable foreign design can change extensively when another navy adapts it to its missions.

evidence.note: Korea already possessed major industrial infrastructure but still needed design teams and personnel familiar with naval technology.
Differing national requirements illustrated by the American redesign of the FREMM-derived Constellation class.

segments.summary: South Korea already had major shipyards. It still needed naval design teams that could adapt foreign technology to Korean geography and missions.

segments.title: Internal consensus may explain steady Korean naval procurement
segments.body: South Korean naval policy has not depended on a few long-serving admirals. Admiral Choi Yun-Hee became the first Republic of Korea Navy officer to chair the Joint Chiefs of Staff in October 2013, then served until 7 October 2015. Regular changes in senior naval leadership make consistent procurement a better guide to sustained strategic priorities than individual tenure. One explanation is that internal debate has allowed the navy to present a consensus externally while the army retains its leading security role. Later rotation of non-army chairmanships between naval and air-force officers suggests increasing maritime influence. This interpretation concerns the consistency of actual purchases, which can differ from policy publications and public political positions.

evidence.note: Admiral Choi Yun-Hee's rise accompanied stronger maritime strategy without showing that senior naval officers had simply displaced the army.
Internal discussion and external consensus are offered as an interpretation of procurement consistency, followed by the rotation of non-army joint chiefs chairmanships.

segments.summary: Consistent procurement suggests that internal debate and an externally presented consensus have helped sustain maritime priorities despite regular leadership changes.

segments.title: Heavy industry becomes a constituency for maritime strategy
segments.body: South Korea's heavy industry supplies the navy and depends on the sea routes that the fleet protects. That combination recalls the political constituency around Britain's Navy League era. Defence contracts give major firms a direct interest in naval spending, while disruption at sea would also threaten their manufacturing and export businesses. Their support therefore reaches beyond contractor lobbying. As alliances become more openly transactional, this domestic constituency strengthens the case that sea-power investment serves national economic interests.

evidence.note: Heavy industry strengthens the navy's influence because it sells to the service and depends on protected trade routes.
Increasingly transactional alliances and the navy's ability to leverage this environment for respect and investment.

segments.summary: Korean industrial firms support naval investment both as suppliers and as businesses whose global trade routes need protection.

segments.title: Hyundai and Hanwha anchor KDX construction
segments.body: Hyundai Heavy Industries and Hanwha Ocean, formerly Daewoo Shipbuilding and Marine Engineering, are the two principal KDX builders. Hanwha Group, formerly the Korean Explosives Company, had already acquired Samsung's aerospace division, which became Hanwha Aerospace. Hanwha Ocean took its present name after the group acquired Daewoo Shipbuilding following an accounting-fraud scandal and trading suspension. The takeover had help from the Korea Development Bank. Both Hyundai and Hanwha Ocean also hold master ship-repair agreements with the US Navy's Naval Supply Systems Command. Daewoo led initial KDX construction in the 1990s, while Hyundai became heavily involved with the second class and later dominated much of the program. Their role ties South Korea's destroyer fleet to shipyards whose work extends beyond domestic new construction.

evidence.note: Hyundai and Hanwha Ocean, formerly Daewoo Shipbuilding, are the principal builders behind the KDX programme.
Hanwha's acquisition of Daewoo Shipbuilding and the two builders' US Navy master ship-repair agreements.

segments.summary: Hyundai Heavy Industries and Hanwha Ocean anchor KDX construction while corporate consolidation and US Navy repair agreements widen their naval role.

segments.title: Cancelled variants and long gaps interrupt KDX development
segments.body: KDX did not follow a smooth production ladder. A proposed Aegis-equipped development of the Chungmugong Yi Sun-sin class was never built, so planned capability did not always reach construction. A decade separates the last first-batch Sejong's commissioning in 2012 from Jeongjo the Great's launch in 2022. Their related external appearance masks major changes in launcher counts, weapon arrangement, and internal fit. The comparison with the Hornet and Super Hornet conveys the scale of the redesign and the case for treating the ships as separate builds.

evidence.note: A planned Aegis-equipped Chungmugong Yi Sun-sin variant was not built and KDX capability arrived inconsistently.
The ten-year gap and extensive weapons-layout changes, comparing the relationship to Hornet and Super Hornet.
The later passage clarifies the ten-year comparison as commissioning in 2012 to Jeongjo the Great's launch in 2022, rather than two commissioning dates.

segments.summary: The Korean destroyer program was progressive without being continuous: an Aegis KDX-II variant disappeared and a decade separated major Sejong-derived builds.

segments.title: Armistice and maritime dependence shape Korean naval priorities
segments.body: The Korean War ended in an armistice rather than a peace treaty, leaving South Korea exposed to renewed conflict with an unpredictable North Korea. At the same time, the country depends on its sea lines of communication and exclusive economic zone. The sea also provides defensive depth around the peninsula. Fleet development must balance the immediate land threat with protection of the ocean routes that sustain the economy. That combination explains why maritime strength remains necessary even while the army holds the leading place in national defence.

evidence.note: South Korea's security priorities combine the unresolved land war and North Korean threat with protection of sea lines of communication, its exclusive economic zone, and maritime defensive depth.

segments.summary: South Korea must prepare for renewed land war while protecting the trade routes and maritime depth on which the peninsula depends.

segments.title: Commercial shipbuilding sustains KDX skills between naval batches
segments.body: Destroyer-order gaps do not leave Hyundai and Hanwha without work. Their enormous shipbuilding complexes produce merchant ships and do not depend on a continuous stream of naval contracts. Commercial production keeps skilled workforces employed and yards engaged with current technology and competitive methods. Warships bring extra scrutiny and may displace more profitable commercial work, but they draw on an industrial base that is already active. South Korea can therefore return to sophisticated combatant production after a pause without rebuilding shipyard competence from scratch.

evidence.note: The builders continue producing merchant ships and are not dependent on Korean naval orders for their livelihood.
Constant commercial production linked to workforce capability, modern technology, and competitive yard practices.

segments.summary: Korea can tolerate gaps in destroyer orders because Hyundai and Hanwha retain skilled workers, modern yards, and production discipline through commercial shipbuilding.

segments.title: Gwanggaeto the Great starts as a practical ASW destroyer
segments.body: The Gwanggaeto the Great class is a capable first indigenous destroyer with a practical anti-submarine role. Sea Sparrow, sixteen Harpoon missiles, a 5-inch gun, Goalkeeper close-in weapons, torpedoes, and Super Lynx helicopters give it a useful general-purpose fit as well. Raytheon and Signaal radars, a BAE combat system, and nuclear, biological, and chemical protection support its claim to be a destroyer rather than a lightly armed large frigate. The lead ship entered service in July 1998 and remained useful after upgrades, approaching twenty-eight years in service when this video was recorded in May 2026. The Super Lynx helicopters are its primary submarine-hunting weapons. They can also engage missile boats and other littoral threats, including acting as gunships with missile pods, which makes them broader all-rounders than the more specialised Seahawk or Merlin configurations discussed here. That versatility suits ships expected to move between coastal and oceanic operations.

evidence.note: The first KDX class is an ASW destroyer equipped with Sea Sparrow, Harpoon, Goalkeeper, torpedoes, sensors, and an integrated combat system.
The section says the class remains useful after decades in service and explains the Super Lynx helicopter as an all-rounder for littoral and oceanic work.

segments.summary: The first KDX class is a solid anti-submarine destroyer that blends imported systems with growing Korean integration skill.

segments.title: Multiple suppliers build Korean systems-integration skill
segments.body: Korea's preference for Goalkeeper includes the suppressive value attributed to its 30 mm cannon. Broadening access to suppliers and technology offers another possible explanation for that choice. Buying every component from one country would simplify integration while leaving Korea dependent on that market and its design assumptions. Combining equipment from different countries develops the skill needed to connect their systems. The resulting independence lies in choosing among suppliers and integrating their equipment, without requiring every component to be invented domestically.

evidence.note: Korea's preference for Goalkeeper and the value of broadening access to suppliers and technology.
Integrating systems from different nations teaches the connections needed for genuine design independence.

segments.summary: Goalkeeper's 30 mm cannon appeals for its suppressive fire, while supplier diversity offers a possible additional reason for Korea's equipment choices.

segments.title: Submarines deny the sea while surface ships exercise control
segments.body: South Korea's submarines are central to naval operations, especially sea denial. They can stop an opponent from using a maritime area, while sea control requires a navy to move forces, sustain commerce, and launch operations through it. A submarine cannot provide air defence for a merchant convoy. Surface combatants are therefore still needed to escort shipping and protect movement. The distinction explains why an expanding submarine force does not remove the requirement for multi-purpose destroyers.

evidence.note: Submarines can deny an enemy use of the sea, while surface ships provide control by escorting and protecting shipping and allowing a navy to operate there.

segments.summary: Submarines can obstruct enemy use of the sea, while surface ships escort shipping and let a navy use the area directly.

segments.title: KDX-II combines Mark 41 and Korean VLS in a multipurpose destroyer
segments.body: The Chungmugong Yi Sun-sin class is the multipurpose KDX-II generation. Its missile battery combines thirty-two Mark 41 cells for SM-2 with twenty-four Korean VLS cells that can carry Red Shark anti-submarine weapons and Hyunmoo-3 land-attack missiles. Those launchers provide 56 VLS cells, with eight SSM-700K Haeseong anti-ship missiles bringing the combined count to 64. One RAM launcher forward, one Goalkeeper aft, and a 5-inch gun complete the weapons fit described for the 6,520-ton full-load ship. Korea's own VLS distinguishes this program from navies that rely on Mark 41 or Sylver despite greater spending or a stronger maritime emphasis. The combination gives KDX-II weapons for several missions while extending Korea's domestic equipment capability.

evidence.note: The 6,520-ton KDX-II carries thirty-two Mark 41 and twenty-four Korean VLS cells for SM-2, Red Shark, and Hyunmoo weapons, plus RAM, Goalkeeper, eight Haeseong missiles, and a 5-inch gun.

segments.summary: The Chungmugong Yi Sun-sin class combines 56 VLS cells with eight deck-launched anti-ship missiles on a 6,520-ton destroyer.

segments.title: A late KDX-II upgrade points to roughly forty years of service
segments.body: The KDX-II improvement program is scheduled for completion by 2033, long after the class entered service between 2003 and 2008. Completing a major upgrade so late would offer little service afterwards if the ships retired after only thirty years. The schedule therefore supports an expectation of roughly forty-year careers. That is an inference from the investment timetable, with the ships' eventual ability to reach that age still an open question. Upgrade timing helps reveal how long a navy expects to retain an existing design.

evidence.note: The improvement project's 2033 completion target and 2003-2008 commissioning dates underpin an inferred forty-year service life, with doubt left about whether the ships will reach it.

segments.summary: A 2033 improvement deadline makes more sense for ships expected to serve about forty years than for a class due to retire after thirty.

segments.title: French stealth influence and Sejong's Burke-like silhouette
segments.body: Some reports describe variation in KDX-II's Korean VLS configuration, which is plausible as an indigenous design develops. Its reduced-signature shaping drew in part on the French La Fayette-class frigates, an influence carried into later Korean builds. Sejong the Great's resemblance to an enlarged Arleigh Burke prompts a separate point: similar equipment can favour similar superstructures and layouts. That resemblance may also create tactical ambiguity over which vessel an opponent is observing.

evidence.note: The transcript qualifies Korean VLS configuration variants as reported, then separately identifies La Fayette influence on reduced-signature shaping.
Similar systems and superstructures create tactical ambiguity, with Sejong described as an enlarged Arleigh Burke.

segments.summary: La Fayette influenced Korean reduced-signature shaping, while Sejong's resemblance to an enlarged Arleigh Burke raises a separate argument about tactical ambiguity.

segments.title: Sejong the Great scales up the Burke-shaped destroyer idea
segments.body: Sejong the Great enlarges a familiar Aegis-destroyer pattern to suit South Korea's fleet economics. Korea planned six of these large destroyers, while the US Navy requires dozens of Arleigh Burkes, so South Korea can justify greater investment in each hull. In the illustrative comparison, spending a Sejong-sized budget on every Burke could leave the US Navy with forty ships where it needs fifty. Greater capability per ship would then come at the expense of needed hull numbers. The diminishing-returns argument is that moving from a highly capable design toward theoretical perfection becomes disproportionately expensive, much as additional ship speed demands rapidly increasing power. Different fleet sizes therefore produce different procurement choices even when both navies value similar technology.

evidence.note: The transcript presents Sejong the Great as a larger Burke-like design built in small numbers.
Korea's case for more expensive individual ships compared with the US Navy's need for larger hull numbers.

segments.summary: South Korea's smaller fleet can justify individual destroyers that are larger and more expensive than their US counterparts.

segments.title: Sejong missile density makes the destroyer a fleet shield
segments.body: The first Sejong batch carries forty-eight Mark 41 cells forward and thirty-two aft, for eighty cells before the Korean launcher is counted. The Mark 41 cells are described as loaded with SM-2 Block III and IV missiles. Another forty-eight Korean VLS cells raise the vertical-launch total to 128. Four quadruple anti-ship launchers bring immediate launch capacity to 144 weapons. A 5-inch gun, Goalkeeper, and RAM provide gun and close-in layers around the missile battery. Those numbers challenge proposals that treat forty-eight missiles as sufficient for every high-end destroyer, especially for a navy facing an immediate and heavily armed threat.

evidence.note: Sejong carries eighty Mark 41 cells, forty-eight Korean VLS cells, and sixteen deck-launched anti-ship missiles for 128 vertical cells and 144 weapons ready to launch, plus a 5-inch gun, Goalkeeper, and RAM.

segments.summary: The first Sejong batch combines 80 Mark 41 cells, 48 Korean VLS cells, and 16 deck-launched anti-ship missiles for 144 weapons ready to launch.

segments.title: Hyunmoo-3 gives Sejong a growing land-attack reach
segments.body: The Korean VLS carries Red Shark anti-submarine rockets as well as Hyunmoo-3 conventional land-attack cruise missiles. Hyunmoo-3 is broadly analogous to Tomahawk, with turbofan propulsion and a maximum conventional payload of about 500 kilograms. The first version entered production in 2006, and the 3C had been in production since 2012. The family grew from roughly 500 kilometres to a cited 3,000 kilometres for the 3D variant, with a cited maximum speed of Mach 1.2. One indigenous launcher thus supports both anti-submarine warfare and progressively deeper conventional strike.

evidence.note: Korean VLS accepts Red Shark and the turbofan-powered Hyunmoo-3 cruise missile. Hyunmoo-3 carries a roughly 500-kilogram payload, entered production in 2006, and gained a 3C version produced from 2012.
The Hyunmoo-3 family's range growth from about 500 to 3,000 kilometres and a cited maximum speed of Mach 1.2.

segments.summary: The Korean VLS can carry Red Shark ASROC and the Hyunmoo-3 cruise-missile family, whose later variants extend Korean conventional strike reach to as much as 3,000 kilometres.

segments.title: Korean SAM options support Sejong's fleet air-defence role
segments.body: The Korean VLS is described as accepting both short-range K-SAMs and Korean area-air-defence missiles. Those weapons add domestic surface-to-air options to Sejong's large Mark 41 battery. Their inclusion supports the assessment that the ship's main task is to create an air-defence area in which other forces can operate. Land attack remains useful, but the additional SAM choices emphasise protection of the surrounding force.

evidence.note: Sejong's 48 Korean VLS cells can carry both short-range and area-air-defence K-SAMs; that weapons mix points to a mission of creating an air-defence cordon in which other forces can operate.

segments.summary: Short-range and area-air-defence K-SAM options add to the case for treating Sejong as a defensive centre for other ships and operations.

segments.title: Missile diversity protects the fleet from supply interruption
segments.body: Missile choice is also a logistics and alliance problem. Domestic K-SAM loading options give Korea alternatives if foreign supply is interrupted by diplomacy, interdiction, or attacks on ports and airfields. Multiple sources protect the fleet against alliance friction and physical attacks on the supply chain. Greater compatibility between Mark 41 and Sylver launchers could likewise allow Standard or Aster missiles to substitute when the preferred weapon is unavailable. Possible differences in launch techniques would first have to be resolved for that cross-loading proposal to work. Once a missile can operate from the launcher, its availability in combat can matter more than the performance difference between two systems.

evidence.note: Domestic K-SAM options provide alternatives if diplomatic restrictions or attacks on shipping, airfields, ports, or urban infrastructure disrupt imported missile supplies.
The proposed Standard/Sylver and Aster/Mark 41 interoperability is conditional on overcoming possible launch-method differences, with an available compatible missile preferred to an empty launcher.

segments.summary: Domestic K-SAM options protect Korea against interruptions in imported missile supply and support a wider case for launcher interoperability.

segments.title: Sejong pairs exceptional missile density with two helicopters
segments.body: At 7,650 tons standard displacement and roughly 10,000 tons full load, Sejong the Great entered service among the largest missile destroyers. Its 128 VLS cells exceed the Type 055's cited 112. In the comparison used here, only the much larger Kirov class carries a heavier missile load. Sejong also has space for two Sea Lynx or Seahawk helicopters. That aviation capacity complements the missile battery and suits a destroyer intended for operations farther from the peninsula.

evidence.note: At roughly 10,000 tons full load, Sejong carries 128 VLS cells against the Type 055's cited 112, with only the much larger Kirov carrying more in this comparison.
Space for two Sea Lynx or Seahawk helicopters and its relevance to deep-sea operations.

segments.summary: The 10,000-ton Sejong surpassed the Type 055 in launcher count and added space for two Sea Lynx or Seahawk helicopters suited to deep-sea operations.

segments.title: KVLS-II gives Jeongjo a heavier ballistic-missile role
segments.body: Jeongjo the Great changes the combat profile by making room for a short-range ballistic missile. Hyunmoo-4's cited 800-kilometre range and 2.5-ton payload require the much larger KVLS-II module. Each four-cell module is approximately 3 by 2.4 by 9.8 metres, consuming substantial hull volume. The resulting fit retains forty-eight forward Mark 41 cells, sixteen Korean VLS cells aft, twenty-four KVLS-II cells, and eight deck-launched anti-ship missiles. Immediate launch capacity falls from Sejong's 144 weapons to 96 in exchange for a much heavier strike option.

evidence.note: Hyunmoo-4's cited 800-kilometre range and 2.5-ton payload require KVLS-II modules about 3 by 2.4 by 9.8 metres; Jeongjo's revised fit uses forty-eight Mark 41, sixteen Korean VLS, twenty-four KVLS-II, and eight deck-launched anti-ship missiles, reducing immediate launch capacity from 144 to 96 weapons.

segments.summary: Jeongjo trades some of Sejong's launcher volume for the much larger KVLS-II and an 800-kilometre Hyunmoo-4 ballistic missile with a 2.5-ton payload.

segments.title: Jeongjo's missile-defence role comes with a redesigned battery
segments.body: South Korea has considered SM-3 for sea-based ballistic-missile defence and support to ground-based defences. Lockheed Martin says the ships can perform integrated air and missile defence, although it is also selling the system. Jeongjo's missile battery is not interchangeable with Sejong's despite related sensors, hull form, and propulsion. Ten years separate the 2012 commissioning of the last first-batch ship from Jeongjo's 2022 launch, leaving time for extensive redesign. The 'batch two' label is administratively convenient, but the changed weapons fit makes the ships operationally distinct in this assessment.

evidence.note: SM-3 use remains possible, while Lockheed Martin's claim that the ships can perform integrated air and missile defence is qualified by the company's commercial interest.
The changed missile fit and ten-year gap support treating Jeongjo as a distinct build despite its batch-two label.

segments.summary: Possible SM-3 integration supports missile defence, while the changed weapons fit and the decade between earlier-batch commissioning in 2012 and Jeongjo's launch in 2022 support treating it as a distinct design.

segments.title: Pairing Sejong and Jeongjo for defence and strike
segments.body: Sejong's large defensive magazine made it an exceptionally powerful air-defence destroyer. Jeongjo has less air-defence depth, but its heavier missiles provide a strike capability the earlier ship lacks. The resulting analogy casts Sejong as the shield and Jeongjo as the spear. Operating them together could combine those strengths in one task group. This is an argument for complementary employment, with each design compensating for a limitation of the other.

evidence.note: The transcript calls Sejong the better shield, Jeongjo the better spear, and their tandem operation a strong task-group combination.

segments.summary: Sejong retains the deeper defensive magazine while Jeongjo supplies the heavier strike weapon, making the two designs complementary rather than direct replacements.

segments.title: Hypersonic weapons and large VLS modules push hull size upward
segments.body: Future Korean weapons may push surface-combatant size beyond Jeongjo. Combining a strong defensive magazine with launchers for hypersonic or other heavy weapons imposes large volume and stability demands. A smaller hull cannot absorb those demands indefinitely. The forecast therefore points toward a larger ship instead of continual missile growth within the same displacement. The payload requirements drive the platform size.

evidence.note: The transcript predicts a larger Korean ship because the size of VLS systems for future hypersonic weapons requires a more stable platform.

segments.summary: Future Korean missiles may require a ship larger than Jeongjo because long, heavy launch modules impose stability and integration demands on the hull.

segments.title: A balanced fleet rejects small-ship-only doctrine
segments.body: Post-Cold War cuts left many navies short of smaller combatants, and those forces need rebuilding. Large ships remain necessary for magazine depth, sensors, and heavy weapons. The Jeune École provides the historical warning: opponents answered small attack craft with rapid-fire guns, including guns carried by smaller escorts of their own. A fleet that builds large ships can still add numerous small vessels around them. A small-ship-only force cannot produce the missing large-ship capabilities when they are needed, so balance matters more than choosing one size category.

evidence.note: Navies need to rebuild small-ship forces while retaining a balance of large and small vessels rather than reviving a small-ship-only Jeune École.
Rapid-fire guns as a response to Jeune École craft, with big-ship fleets also able to field small ships.

segments.summary: Rebuilding small combatants after post-Cold War cuts is necessary, but the historical Jeune École warning is that small ships cannot substitute for every large-ship function.

segments.title: Jeongjo's strike role raises a close-in defence question
segments.body: Jeongjo the Great's Phalanx fit raises a close-in defence question after Korea's long use of Goalkeeper. Fewer navies now sustain Goalkeeper, which helps explain the industrial choice, but RAM could add another defensive layer. Jeongjo's ballistic-missile strike capacity makes it a priority target and increases the importance of terminal defence. Multiple RAM launchers alongside Phalanx would be one way to strengthen that protection. Its survivability also depends on the surrounding formation. A nearby Sejong contributes a deep defensive magazine, and additional escorts can add more layers around the task group.

evidence.note: The transcript weighs Phalanx against RAM and identifies Jeongjo as a priority target because of its strike capacity.
A nearby Sejong and additional escorts would provide a deep layered defensive magazine.

segments.summary: A high-value ballistic-missile destroyer becomes an obvious target, so its Phalanx fit is weighed against RAM and layered escort protection.

segments.title: Korean task groups may answer Japan's carriers and cruisers
segments.body: South Korea already fields strong surface-action groups and substantial amphibious capability. Competition with Japan may shape the next step as Japan builds cruiser-sized combatants, converts ships into carriers, and organises task groups around them. A Korean carrier-like group would provide a mobile airfield and could create an offensive and defensive bubble along the China Sea approaches. It could complicate an opponent's route toward Korea while protecting trade routes and sea lines of communication. The same force would give Seoul limited regional expeditionary capability beyond direct defence of the peninsula.

evidence.note: The closing section covers Korean surface-action and amphibious capability, competition with Japanese carriers and cruisers, a mobile airfield, protection of maritime approaches, and regional expeditionary utility.

segments.summary: Existing surface-action and amphibious forces give South Korea a base for carrier-like task groups that could protect trade and avoid being outmatched by Japanese naval aviation.
